sentences: Planes of colour in many different shapes overlap and lock together across the surface.
Green, black, red and ochre pieces lean at angles, holding one another up.
The whole thing stands like a single building.
The Russian avant-garde artist Lyubov Popova joined Malevich's Suprematist group Supremus in 1916.
She went on to paint a series she called Painterly Architectonics, and this 1918 picture belongs to it.
At the top, a large black quadrilateral rests at a slant over a red ground.
Its edges tilt as if they might push past the frame.
Search as you like: you will find almost no true verticals or horizontals here.
On the left, a long green plane leans beside a black one.
Try to work out which plane lies on top and which slips beneath: follow the order of the overlaps.
A shallow depth opens up on a flat surface.
At the centre a red triangle rises, and beside it a grey glow spreads like mist.
That light seeming to seep out between the planes is the focal point.
It feels as if air were moving between the solid shapes.
Now come in close to the broad ochre plane near the bottom.
The paint stands up thickly, its rough grain left untouched.
Each plane has its own brushmarks and texture, so even flat shapes feel different in weight.
Let your eyes rest on the white ground and the small green shard at lower right.
This picture is painted on cardboard, not canvas.
The thickly raised white paint makes even the background look like a building material.
As the word architectonic suggests, she treated each plane of colour almost as solid material, building relationships in which parts prop up or push against each other.
The series joins Malevich's colour planes with the relief constructions of Vladimir Tatlin, in whose Moscow studio she worked around 1912.
Born into a wealthy textile merchant's family, she studied with Cubist painters in Paris in 1912 and 1913.
She was also deeply drawn to ancient Russian icons and to the paintings of Giotto.
In 1921, with fellow artists, she declared easel painting finished and turned to applied arts such as textile design.
In 1924 she died of scarlet fever, caught from her son, just two days after his death.
She was thirty-five.
Finally, step back and imagine pulling one plane out of the picture.
Would the whole structure collapse?
The answer holds the very principle of Popova's painterly architecture.
